strengths: Excellent problem diagnosis with rigorous empirical analysis: Section 3.3 provides clear evidence that pretrained DiT heads exhibit sharp phase selectivity near Δ≈0, establishing RoPE phase mismatch as root cause of mixed-resolution failures

Elegant and principled solution: CRPA is training-free, parameter-free, and based on the simple 'one attention, one scale' principle that directly addresses phase coherence; minimal computational overhead (0.3%) with compatibility for any pretrained DiT

Comprehensive experimental validation across two distinct models (Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev) with multiple metrics (DOVER, VBench, FID, CLIP-IQA), diverse RoPE baselines, and extensive ablations in supplementary material
Kernel decomposition insight (Eq. 6) provides intuitive interpretation of attention behavior as mixture of sinusoidal phase kernels, connecting empirical observations to theoretical understanding

Strong practical value: training-free drop-in fix for real efficiency bottleneck in diffusion inference; demonstrates compatibility with orthogonal acceleration methods (Tables 4-5); works with arbitrary LR/HR layouts and irregular masks
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvement over strongest baseline: RALU comparison shows only ~1.4% FID improvement (32.45 vs 32.91 in Table 3); no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided, making it unclear if gains are robust or within noise margins

Limited theoretical justification for kernel form (Eq. 6): assumes content averaging but does not rigorously validate this approximation or establish when it accurately characterizes learned behavior; connection to sampling theory (phase aliasing, Nyquist) is intuitive but not formalized

Boundary Expand-and-Replace component feels orthogonal: requires training 6-25M parameter upsampler models; ablation shows only ~0.3% improvement (Table 8); suggests main problem solved by CRPA alone, making overall contribution less unified

Restricted evaluation scope: only 2 DiT models tested; resolution mixing limited to 2:1 ratios; no experiments with extreme ratios (4:1, 8:1) or other positional encodings (ALiBi, XPos); generalization unclear

Acknowledged but unresolved limitations: Section E admits fine details in ultra-high-resolution regions remain unstable; attributed to training data but represents practical ceiling; Figure 13 (480p+1920p) lacks rigorous quality assessment

Missing critical ablations: no visualization of attention weight changes with/without CRPA; no analysis of which heads benefit most; limited boundary band size study (only n_pad ∈ {0,2,4}); no systematic study of HR token ratio selection across different scenarios

Saliency detection dependency adds complexity: DeepGazeIIE [60] is potential failure point; Table 9 shows 0.6% overhead; no robustness analysis for poor saliency predictions or comparison of alternative methods
Statistical rigor lacking: no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests across multiple seeds; single random seed results make it difficult to assess robustness of improvements

strengths: Novel problem identification: Clearly identifies and diagnoses RoPE phase aliasing as the failure mode in mixed-resolution denoising, providing valuable empirical evidence that pretrained DiT heads implement sharply-tuned, multi-frequency phase kernels (Eq. 6 and Fig. 3)

Elegant practical solution: CRPA is training-free, requires minimal modifications to existing code, and demonstrably improves generation quality without retraining, making it immediately applicable to deployed models

Comprehensive experimental validation: Tests on both video (Wan2.1) and image (FLUX) models with extensive baselines (PI-LR/HR, NTK, YaRN, RALU) and multiple evaluation metrics (DOVER, VBench, FID, MUSIQ, CLIP-IQA)

Clear presentation of core insight: Section 3.3 effectively demonstrates that attention scores depend intricately on consistent phase sampling through kernel decomposition, with clean visualizations of the learned phase preferences
Practical empirical results: Achieves performance approaching the two-stage upper bound while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to mixed-resolution baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in core contribution: Once the phase mismatch problem is identified, the solution (re-indexing positions to query's reference grid) is relatively straightforward and lacks deeper algorithmic innovation. The gap between problem diagnosis and solution is small

Unjustified design choices: Why the query's scale for reference frame selection is optimal is never explained theoretically or empirically. No comparison with alternatives (average scale, geometric mean, fixed frequency scale), making this appear as an engineering choice rather than principled design

Incomplete Boundary Expand-and-Replace justification: The lightweight neural component contradicts the 'training-free drop-in fix' claim, adds 2.9% overhead, and its necessity—despite CRPA—suggests the core solution is incomplete. Only 3 ablation settings tested (0,0), (2,2), (2,4)

Confounded contributions: Results depend on both CRPA fixing phase alignment AND saliency-based region selection. The paper doesn't isolate these contributions or show CRPA's standalone impact. Sensitivity to saliency detector quality is unexamined

Insufficient problem analysis: Why pretrained heads develop sharp phase selectivity is unexplored. Relationship to RoPE extrapolation literature is underdeveloped—why don't similar issues manifest in language models with heterogeneous contexts?

Limited generalization scope: Untested on >2 resolution levels, only two model families, unclear handling of 2D separable rotations and cross-axis phase interactions, and no evaluation on non-RoPE positional encodings

Metric noise and missing statistical analysis: FID differences (32.08 vs. 32.45) are within typical noise; no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported. Small improvements in CLIP-IQA (0.563 vs. 0.556) lack significance testing

Confounded saliency mechanism: The practical pipeline depends heavily on the saliency detector (DeepGazeIIE) but sensitivity to detection quality is unexamined. Difficult to separate CRPA's contribution from importance-based scheduling benefits
Incomplete 2D/3D analysis: Derivation is 1D; images use separable rotations per axis. Whether phase alignment holds across axes and potential axis-specific failure modes are not discussed

Acknowledged unresolved limitations: Section E admits ultra-high-resolution details become unstable when models lack training on such resolutions, representing a substantive limitation for high-fidelity applications that is not solved by this work

strengths: Thorough and insightful problem diagnosis (Section 3): Clear identification of RoPE phase mismatch as root cause of mixed-resolution attention collapse, supported by both mathematical analysis (Eq. 6) and compelling empirical evidence (Figure 3)

Elegant and principled solution: The 'one attention, one scale' principle directly addresses the diagnosed problem via simple index remapping; training-free and drop-in compatible with pretrained models

Comprehensive experimental validation: Strong results on two distinct models (Wan2.1, FLUX) across multiple metrics (DOVER, VBench, FID, CLIP-IQA, MUSIQ); consistent improvements over multiple RoPE interpolation baselines
Practical impact and efficiency: Achieves quality competitive with full-resolution baselines (e.g., ~99.6 DOVER vs 99.8 for HR) while being ~4× faster; minimal computational overhead (<0.3%)

Well-structured presentation and reproducibility: Clear narrative flow, effective visualizations, detailed implementation specifications, thorough supplementary material with derivations and ablations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: CRPA is essentially index remapping—a straightforward engineering solution rather than a fundamental algorithmic innovation; core contribution is problem diagnosis rather than method

Boundary Expand-and-Replace feels ad-hoc: Requires training separate model-specific upsampler networks, introduces additional hyperparameters (npad), addresses symptom rather than root cause; modest empirical gains (Table 8)

Narrow scope and generalizability: Only tested on two DiT models; unclear how approach generalizes to other architectures or positional encoding schemes; importance-based region selection relies on external saliency detection

Incomplete failure mode analysis: Limited systematic exploration of when/why CRPA might fail; instability in ultra-high-resolution details attributed to training data feels incomplete; no analysis of multi-scale scenarios with >2 resolutions

Theoretical gaps: Why do DiT heads develop such sharp periodic phase selectivity? Is this fundamental or training-artifact? Transitions from theory (Eq. 6) to empirical analysis (Section 3.3) could be more rigorous; RoPE-dominance score threshold (0.085) not justified

Limited architectural scope and saturation: Quality-cost curve (Figure 9) shows rapid saturation >40% high-res tokens, limiting applicability for high-resolution-critical tasks; unclear practical benefit in bandwidth-limited scenarios

strengths: Novel theoretical identification of RoPE's sinusoidal scale bias problem in mixed-resolution settings with rigorous mathematical analysis (Sections 3.2-3.3 and Equation 6)
Training-free solution that requires no model retraining, making it immediately practical for any pre-trained RoPE-based diffusion model

Comprehensive experimental validation spanning video generation (Wan2.1, multi-resolution) and image generation (FLUX) with consistent improvements across multiple quality metrics (DOVER, VBench, ImageReward)
Extensive ablation studies examining BER design choices, saliency models, subsampling strategies, and multi-resolution configurations
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Fig. 3 demonstrating empirical sinusoidal bias and Figs. 15-16 showing learned attention deviations from theory)
Broad applicability demonstrated across 2K/4-mixed resolution scenarios and integration with orthogonal acceleration techniques
Careful treatment of related work distinguishing this contribution from prior position interpolation methods (NTK, YaRN, etc.)
weaknesses: Boundary Expand-and-Replace (BER) module lacks rigorous theoretical justification—design choices (bidirectional exchange, dilation factors) appear empirically driven rather than principled, reducing confidence in optimal design

Persistent unresolved failure cases at complex LR-HR texture boundaries (Fig. 17: ski slopes, giraffes, forests) with incomplete proposed solutions, limiting applicability to unconstrained real-world scenarios
Computational overhead of PMA position rescaling not clearly quantified—Table 16 breaks down components but doesn't isolate the cost of local rescaling during inference or GPU memory implications
Evaluation scope limited primarily to diffusion models; claims of general RoPE applicability would be strengthened by evaluation on language models or other RoPE-based architectures
Insufficient analysis of how learned attention biases differ across modalities and content types most affected by phase misalignment—deeper characterization of failure modes beyond visual examples
External dependency on saliency models for importance-based region selection (Section 4.3) with limited exploration of sensitivity to model choice or design guidelines for this application
Incomplete comparison with non-interpolation approaches—missing comparisons with methods that natively support multi-resolution from design (e.g., hierarchical or conditional attention mechanisms)

strengths: Clear mathematical analysis of RoPE's failure under mixed-resolution settings, with effective visualization of sinusoidal scale bias through κ(Δ) curves
Practical training-free solution (PMA) requiring no architectural modifications, immediately applicable to existing models
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (Wan 2.1, FLUX) and diverse evaluation metrics (DOVER, VBench, CLIP-IQA, ImageReward)
Thorough ablation studies and integration tests demonstrating compatibility with existing acceleration techniques
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation specifications and hyperparameters for all baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: rescaling positions per token-pair to enforce consistent scales is a straightforward engineering fix lacking algorithmic depth
Marginal empirical improvements across metrics (0.25-5.6% in most cases, without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals)
Unresolved fundamental limitation: Section E and Figure 17 show the method still produces artifacts at complex LR-HR boundaries, undermining claims of stability
Insufficient theoretical justification: paper demonstrates empirically that rescaling helps but lacks rigorous analysis of why this specific strategy is optimal or convergence guarantees

Incomplete comparison with related work: RALU [44], the closest prior on mixed-resolution generation, lacks direct quantitative comparison; overstatement of novelty as 'first to focus on mixed-resolution'
Contradictory claims: method is described as 'training-free' but includes BER module requiring trained latent up/downsampler networks; interaction between PMA and BER under-explored
Questionable design choices: reliance on off-the-shelf salience detectors (DeepGaze) appears ad-hoc; different baseline configurations per model complicates fair comparison
Presentation issues: dense writing obscures key insights; κ(Δ) analysis uses small fonts; connection between sinusoidal bias theory and actual attention mechanism under-explained
Missing ablations: no justification for choice of reference scale; no analysis of failure case frequency; no comparison with alternative rescaling strategies
Potential selection bias: extensive prompt list in Appendix F suggests cherry-picking for qualitative results

strengths: Novel theoretical analysis identifying RoPE's sinusoidal scale bias as a fundamental limitation in mixed-resolution attention, with rigorous mathematical formulation (κ(Δ) analysis) and empirical validation across axes
Elegant training-free solution (PMA) requiring only position remapping without architectural changes or additional parameters, enabling straightforward integration into pre-trained models

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (video and image generation), diverse metrics (DOVER, VBench, ImgReward, CLIP variants), and extensive comparisons with RoPE variants and acceleration methods

Thorough ablation studies quantifying contributions of each component (Tables 7, 15, 16) and exploring extensions (multi-resolution scaling, ultra-high-resolution, integration with orthogonal acceleration techniques)
Clear presentation with effective motivation combining intuitive visualization (Fig. 3) and mathematical rigor, making the problem and solution accessible
Consistent empirical improvements demonstrated across all tested scenarios (+1.95 DOVER on video, comparable gains on images) with well-documented quality-speed trade-offs
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in solution components: PMA's position rescaling is straightforward once the κ(Δ) problem is identified; BER uses standard upsampler/downsampler architecture; salience-guided denoising is orthogonal to main contribution
Incomplete handling of failure modes: Section E acknowledges persistent artifacts at LR-HR boundaries (Fig. 17) but proposes only segmentation as future work without implementation or evaluation

Reduced 'training-free' scope: While PMA is training-free, BER requires paired training data and salience-guided approach depends on external pre-trained models, narrowing the full training-free claim

Insufficient justification for design choices: boundary padding (2 tokens) lacks ablation; why HR is the reference scale when HR is query position lacks theoretical motivation; PMA computational overhead not quantified

Theoretical gaps: While κ(Δ) oscillations are rigorously demonstrated, the causal connection to visual artifacts remains empirical; why sinusoidal phase mismatch inherently causes degradation not fully explained

Limited evaluation scope: Experiments restricted to text-to-image/video with transformer DITs; no evaluation on other architectures, position encodings, or domains; no comparison with fixed-scale baselines
Unclear novelty boundaries: Claims of being 'first to focus on mixed-resolution generation' partially contradicted by RALU [44] prior work; distinction could be clearer
